# FCA Focus on Unlogged Complaints in UK Insurers

![View profile for Elliott Crosby]()

Your QA team reviewed 47 calls last week. The FCA wants to talk about the other 953.
That's the maths most UK insurers are living with right now.
3-5% sampling, and hoping the 95% they didn't hear wasn't the 95% that mattered.
Complaints that went unlogged. Vulnerable customers who didn't get the right outcome. Consumer Duty gaps that nobody spotted because nobody listened.
Here's the thing: the FCA isn't interested in how hard your QA team worked. It's interested in outcomes.
And "we sampled our best calls" isn't the audit trail anyone wants to be defending.
The contact centres I speak to are handling some genuinely complex stuff. Medical declarations. Non-standard risks. Customers in financial difficulty being chased on renewals.
These aren't the interactions you can afford to miss. They're exactly the ones you can't.
At [Capacity](https://www.linkedin.com/company/teamcapacity?trk=public_post-text), we help insurance operations teams monitor 100% of conversations.
Not the ones QA had time to get to. All of them.
Automated post-call scoring. Real-time agent guidance. Vulnerability flags.
The kind of audit-ready evidence that makes a Consumer Duty review feel like a normal Tuesday rather than a fire drill.
QA teams stop drowning in call listening rotas and start actually improving things. Managers can evidence outcomes without scrambling for data the night before a visit.
If you're running a contact centre or claims operation and QA still means spreadsheets and a rota, I'd love to show you what it looks like when it doesn't.
Drop me a message. Happy to share what we're seeing across the market.

## More Relevant Posts

I've changed my mind about what the insurance board report problem actually is. I used to think it was about sampling rates.
The FCA has six open investigations right now, two in insurance. They're asking what actually happened to customers on the calls. Not whether the process ran.
For a 30-seat broker, the QA team checks about 400 calls a month out of 8,000. The board signs a report on those 400. The other 7,600 nobody ever heard. The attestation covers 8,000. The evidence covers 400.
I think the people writing those reports know the gap is there. They sign on a sample and hope the rest looks similar. I'm not sure that holds up to six open investigations.
I built insights360 to close that gap. So the attestation and the evidence cover the same calls.
Where am I wrong on this?

A thought-provoking observation from the insurance industry:
"Customers rarely judge insurers on routine transactions. They judge them when something unusual happens."
Most policies are issued without issues. Most claims follow established processes. The real test comes when a case falls outside the standard workflow—an unusual claim, a documentation gap, a policy interpretation issue, or a service request requiring urgent intervention.
This is where insurers, brokers, agents, surveyors, and TPAs all have a role to play.
As insurance professionals, perhaps the next level of customer experience is not just improving turnaround times for routine cases, but strengthening our ability to handle exceptions with speed, empathy, and clear communication.
In general insurance, trust is built not when everything goes as expected, but when it doesn't.
What are your views? Is exception handling the most important differentiator in insurance service today?

"Regulatory enforcement is most effective when it is transparent, predictable and proportionate. IRDAI's proposed Penalty Regulations, 2026 seek to institutionalize these principles across the insurance ecosystem."
IRDAI's Proposed Penalty Framework 2026: A Shift Towards Predictable and Principle-Based Enforcement
The release of the Exposure Draft on the IRDAI (Manner and Procedure for Imposing Penalties) Regulations, 2026 marks an important milestone in the evolution of insurance regulation in India.
While insurers and intermediaries have long been subject to regulatory actions under the Insurance Act, 1938 and the IRDA Act, 1999, the proposed framework seeks to formally codify the process governing regulatory enforcement and penalty imposition.
From an industry perspective, the significance lies not merely in the power to impose penalties, but in the clarity around how such powers will be exercised.
Some notable developments include:
·        Structured triggers for initiating proceedings based on inspections, investigations, audits, complaints and regulatory oversight.
·        Enhanced transparency through detailed Show Cause Notices specifying allegations, evidence relied upon and applicable penalty provisions.
·        Formal recognition of natural justice principles through opportunities for written submissions and personal hearings, including virtual hearings.
·        Requirement for reasoned orders, providing greater clarity on findings and regulatory expectations.
·        Adoption of proportionality as a guiding principle in determining penalties, moving towards risk-based and outcome-focused enforcement.
For insurers, brokers, corporate agents, IMFs, TPAs and other regulated entities, the proposed regulations reinforce the importance of robust compliance management, documentation standards, governance oversight and timely remediation of regulatory observations.
The framework is also expected to improve consistency and predictability in enforcement actions, enabling regulated entities to better assess regulatory risks and strengthen compliance cultures.
As the insurance sector prepares for the broader reforms introduced under the Sabka Bima Sabki Raksha (Amendment of Insurance Laws) Act, 2025, this proposal reflects IRDAI's continued focus on balancing regulatory effectiveness with procedural fairness.
The consultation process presents an important opportunity for industry stakeholders to provide constructive feedback and help shape a modern, transparent and accountable enforcement framework.

Say this with me. A DENIAL IS NOT A NO!
Most independent providers don't know that.
When an insurance remittance arrives flagged as a "denial," many busy practice managers immediately view it as lost revenue or an active write-off decision.
But in the world of high-level Revenue Cycle Management (RCM), we categorize these strictly into two buckets: soft denials and hard denials.
The Soft Denial: This is purely a documentation hurdle. The insurer isn't saying the service isn't covered; they are saying your data didn't clear their rules engine. A missing modifier, an unlinked pre-auth code, or an ambiguous Claim Adjustment Reason Code (CARC) like CO-16 means the claim is completely fixable with the right documentation package.
The Hard Denial: This requires a formal contractual appeal or a direct policy exclusion review. These are the ones that require legal and clinical precision to overturn.
The truth? Up to 90% of medical billing denials are entirely preventable or easily overturned on the first appeal, provided your response relies on the insurer's EXACT internal criteria rather than generic request letters.
Stop treating automated insurer pushback as a final verdict. It's simply the first round of the documentation audit.
What is the most frustrating denial reason you have ever seen? Drop the CARC code below if you know it.

The insurance industry is increasingly recognising that policyholder trust is built not only through products, but through effective grievance resolution and customer-centric governance.
The recent Orientation Programme for Insurance Ombudsmen conducted under the guidance of IRDAI reflects the sector’s growing focus on strengthening institutional capacity, improving consistency in grievance handling, and enhancing the overall efficiency of dispute resolution mechanisms.
Key themes emerging from the discussions included:
• Faster and more accessible complaint resolution
• Reducing delays in grievance registration and disposal
• Tackling recurring instances of mis-selling
• Leveraging digital tools and video hearings
• Improving transparency and policyholder awareness
• Building a more technology-enabled Ombudsman ecosystem
The fact that over 41,000 grievances were resolved during 2025–26, with a significant percentage decided in favour of policyholders, underscores the increasing importance of accountability and trust within the insurance ecosystem.
As insurance penetration expands, grievance management is no longer just a compliance requirement—it is becoming a strategic pillar for long-term customer confidence and industry credibility.
At ElpeeCo. we work with organizations strengthen governance, compliance, and policyholder-centric frameworks while navigating evolving regulatory expectations and operational risk challenges across the insurance sector.
